filled_passage:
Fifteen-year-old Sam volunteers at Green Lane's community food fair. Visitors waiting for meals stood beside the serving table. Their queue blocked the entrance, making it difficult for others to pass.

Sam tried calling names, but several visitors had the same name. "Two people stood up when I called Alex," he recalled. Orders needed to be identified separately.

He made numbered cards and matching flags. Visitors received cards, then sat in a waiting area. When a meal was ready, a server raised the flag with the same number.

Sam initially numbered only one side. Visitors behind the server could see nothing. He numbered the other side too. Wind was another problem: flags kept falling. He added heavier stands to keep them upright, testing them at an empty table before placing them beside food.

During a trial, a visitor lost her card. A server checked her order record to confirm it, then issued a new number. After she collected her meal, staff marked the old number as used to prevent a second collection.

At the next fair, the entrance was clear. Sam reported a change in where people waited, not proof that cooks worked faster. Cooking times had not been measured.

He kept a notebook of problems: fallen flags, lost cards and confusing numbers. It helped him decide what to improve next.

"The first design wasn't the final one," Sam said. Volunteers now test each version before opening. A flag's main purpose is to display a number clearly. Sam hopes the system works even when he is absent and someone else runs the desk.
